options: The OS can run privileged instructions that ordinary programs cannot
The CPU can skip fetch
Every process shares one stack
Compilers can emit interrupts directly into the ALU
questions.explanation: User mode is a cage. Kernel mode is allowed to change page tables, talk to devices, and the like. A trap is the door between them.

questions.prompt: A system call enters the kernel by
options: A controlled trap that switches to kernel mode and jumps to a known entry
An ordinary store into the kernel’s memory
Restarting the machine
Editing the interrupt vector from user mode
questions.explanation: The instruction raises a trap. Hardware flips the privilege level and vectors to the OS entry, which checks the request.
traps: A normal function call does not change privilege.

questions.prompt: Which requests need a system call on a typical OS?
options: Read bytes from an open file
Create a new process
Add two values that are already in registers
End the current process
questions.explanation: File transfer, process creation, and exit cross into the kernel. Adding two registers stays in user mode.
traps: Assuming every library call, including pure arithmetic, is a system call.

questions.prompt: Which instruction should be rejected in user mode?
options: One that disables interrupts
One that adds two registers
One that jumps inside the program
One that shifts a register by one
questions.explanation: Interrupt masking, I/O, and page-table writes are privileged. Arithmetic and local jumps are the program’s own business.

questions.prompt: A C library call such as a formatted print is
options: Often a user-space wrapper that eventually makes a write system call
Itself the kernel
Illegal in user mode
A cache-control instruction
questions.explanation: The library can format the string in user space. Moving the bytes to a terminal still goes through a system call such as write.
traps: Treating the library name and the system call as the same boundary.

questions.prompt: The shell you type commands into is
options: A user-space process that creates other processes
A part of the ALU
The interrupt controller
The page-replacement algorithm
questions.explanation: The shell is an ordinary program. It reads a line, then asks the kernel to create and run another process.

questions.prompt: Compared with a monolithic kernel, a microkernel tries to
options: Keep the privileged core small and run more services outside it
Remove the need for system calls
Put every driver in the ALU
Forbid processes
questions.explanation: Monolithic kernels run file systems and many drivers in kernel mode. A microkernel pushes more of that into separate servers. Both still use a mode switch.

questions.prompt: The privilege level changes during a system call so that
options: The processor may legally execute the kernel’s privileged instructions
The cache is flushed to disk
The program counter stops incrementing forever
User registers are discarded on purpose
questions.explanation: The mode bit, or the equivalent privilege level, is what makes the kernel’s instructions legal. On the way back it must be user mode again.

questions.prompt: What has to be true again when a system call returns normally?
questions.answer: The CPU is back in user mode, the caller can see a return value, and execution resumes after the trap.
questions.explanation: The kernel may have changed kernel data structures. The caller should not come back still privileged, and it needs its registers restored.
